bullets: How to find arc lengths and sector areas, work out the volume of a pyramid from its base and height, use the sphere volume formula, and see why areas scale with the square of the radius
slides.heading: E-Math mensuration: sectors, pyramids and spheres
slides.notes: Welcome everyone in and say: today we measure curved edges and sectors, fill a pyramid and a sphere, and finish by testing what really happens to area when a radius grows.

bullets: Find arc lengths and sector areas as fractions of a full circle
Calculate pyramid and sphere volumes and judge area scaling when the radius changes
slides.heading: What we will learn
slides.notes: Read the goals aloud and tell the class: keep these in mind, because the exit ticket at the end will ask you to do exactly these things.

bullets: A pizza with twice the radius of another - does it hold twice as much topping, or more?
What does the radius control: the edge, the surface, or both?
slides.heading: Twice the radius - how much more pizza?
slides.notes: Ask for a show of hands and take two or three answers without judging them yet; say: the scenes will measure exactly how edges, areas and volumes grow.

bullets: Arc length and sector area are the angle-over-360 fraction of the circumference and the circle area
Pyramid volume is one third of base area times height; sphere volume is 4/3 pi r cubed
slides.heading: Fractions of circles, thirds of prisms, spheres
slides.notes: Say this slowly, because it is the map for the whole lesson: every formula today is a fraction of a familiar whole - a circle, a prism, or a scaling square.

bullets: Sweep the 60 degree sector out of the full circle: it is one sixth of the whole
Arc is 1/6 of 2 pi r and sector area is 1/6 of pi r squared
slides.heading: Arc length and sector area
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: watch the radius sweep the sector open, then read the arc and the sector area off as the same one-sixth fraction of the full circle.

bullets: Fill the pyramid with sand and pour it into the matching prism: it takes three fills
Volume is 1/3 x base area x vertical height
slides.heading: Pyramid volume, revealed
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the pyramid empties into the prism three times before the prism is full, which is where the one third comes from.

bullets: Slice the sphere into thin disks and stack their areas: the total is 4/3 pi r cubed
For r = 3 cm the volume is 36 pi, about 113 cubic centimetres
slides.heading: Sphere volume
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: each thin slice is a disk, and stacking the disks rebuilds the sphere - the radius is cubed because it grows the slice in every direction.

bullets: Grow the radius from 3 cm to 6 cm and the disk fills with four copies of the small one
Area goes from 9 pi to 36 pi: four times, not two times
slides.heading: A common mistake: doubling r doubles area
slides.notes: Narrate the scene as it plays: the doubled radius lays the small disk across the big one twice in each direction, so four small disks fit inside.

bullets: Arc length = 60/360 x 2 pi x 6 = 2 pi, about 6.28 cm
Sector area = 60/360 x pi x 6 squared = 6 pi, about 18.8 square centimetres
slides.heading: Worked example: a 60 degree sector, r = 6 cm
slides.notes: Work through it line by line and keep the fraction 60/360 visible: the same fraction drives both the arc and the area.

bullets: Find the arc length and sector area for a 90 degree sector of radius 8 cm
Find the volume of a square pyramid with base 6 cm by 6 cm and height 4 cm
slides.heading: Your turn
slides.notes: Give three minutes in pairs; the answers are 4 pi cm and 12 pi square centimetres for the sector, and 48 cubic centimetres for the pyramid.

bullets: Three quick questions: a sector fraction, a sphere volume, and the radius-doubling claim
Write your reasoning, not just the number
slides.heading: Exit ticket
slides.notes: Hand out the exit ticket and collect it at the door; the last question revisits the claim we tested in the final scene.
